web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Engine — Discovery CRO, Commercial CDMO & New Modalities
question: What exact services does Sai Life Sciences sell across CRO and CDMO, how does revenue split across modalities and geographies, and what does a real customer engagement look like end to end?

epigraph.quote: A key highlight of our growth continues to be increasing contribution from large pharma... moving to consolidate the full life cycle from early development to commercial manufacturing.
epigraph.author: Krishna Kanumuri, MD & CEO, Sai Life Sciences

web_blocks.title: Two Integrated Engines: Discovery CRO (38%) and Development & Commercial CDMO (62%)

web_blocks.html: Sai Life runs an integrated 'follow-the-molecule' CRDMO model with two reporting pillars [1, 9, 14]. In H1 FY27 (revenue ₹1,213 Cr), Contract Research (CRO / Discovery) generated 38% of revenue. It grew +24% YoY in Q1 FY27 and +28% YoY in Q2 FY27 [7, 9]. Contract Development and Manufacturing (CDMO / CMC) generated 62% of revenue and grew +20% YoY in Q2 FY27 [7, 9]. Rather than running two separate units, Sai Life uses its CRO bench as a feeder into higher-margin, multi-year CDMO supply deals [14, 20].

By geography, 100% of revenue comes from innovator drugs in regulated markets. Roughly 40% comes from the United States, 35% from Europe, 15% from Japan, and 10% from the UK and other developed markets [17]. The firm serves over 300 active innovators, including 18 of the top 25 global pharma companies [18]. Large pharma's share of sales climbed from 28% in FY22 to 49% in FY26 [10]. Global sponsors are cutting vendor counts and picking integrated, audit-ready partners [10, 14].

web_blocks.takeaway: CDMO provides 62% of revenue and commercial scale stability, while CRO (38%) embeds Sai Life inside innovator R&D pipelines years before molecules reach Phase III or commercial launch [9, 14].

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Example 1 (CRO / Discovery): The Schrödinger Computational-to-Bench Engine

web_blocks.html: To see how Sai Life's CRO engine works, look at its five-year deal with Schrödinger, the US computational drug discovery firm [21]. Schrödinger's software designs virtual small-molecule candidates in New York or Cambridge. Even so, digital hits still face a physical hurdle. Chemists must make them in a lab, purify them, run assays, and test metabolic stability (DMPK) before picking a preclinical drug [21].

Under the January 2023 deal, Sai Life built the Sai Schrödinger Research Laboratories (SSRL) at Genome Valley in Hyderabad and opened it in April 2023 [21]. Dedicated full-time equivalent (FTE) teams of chemists, biologists, and analysts work solely on Schrödinger's Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) loops [20, 21]. Schrödinger pays steady FTE fees per scientist-year. In return, Sai Life cuts turnaround time from design to assay without forcing the client to juggle multiple vendors [20, 21]. Because the lab is ring-fenced, IP protection and team know-how compound over five years.

web_blocks.title: Concrete Real-World Example 2 (CDMO / Commercial): Bridging Manchester Route Scouting to Bidar GMP Scale

web_blocks.html: Now trace a late-stage CDMO project for a US or EU sponsor making a complex cancer drug or an Antibody-Drug Conjugate (ADC) payload [13, 19]. Early lab routes that make grams for Phase I trials rarely work at multi-ton commercial scale. They often use unsafe reagents, heavy solvent loads, or costly column purifications.

Sai Life's process chemists at Alderley Park in Manchester, UK work side by side with the client's CMC team to rebuild the synthetic route [19]. They swap batch steps for continuous flow chemistry, photochemistry, or biocatalysis and deliver early kilo batches [6, 14, 19]. As Phase II and III demand grows, the process moves to Unit IV in Bidar, Karnataka. There, 0.25 KL to 12 KL stainless-steel, glass-lined, and Hastelloy reactors—plus OEB 6 isolators for toxic HPAPIs—produce commercial API under USFDA and PMDA clearance [12, 13, 23]. The deal shifts from fee-for-service (FFS) R&D to multi-year per-kg commercial supply across 34 active commercial NCEs and ~160 pipeline programs [12, 20].

web_blocks.title: Next-Generation Modalities: Peptides, ADCs, PROTACs & Oligonucleotide Building Blocks

web_blocks.html: Beyond standard small molecules, Sai Life has invested early in complex new modalities [13]. Driven by GLP-1 metabolic drugs, it opened a Peptide Research Center in Hyderabad with solid-phase, liquid-phase, and hybrid synthesis [13]. In oncology, OEB 6 isolators (containment down to 0.01 µg/m³) handle toxic ADC payloads, GalNAc linkers, and bioconjugation [13]. The firm also makes PROTAC degraders, phosphoramidites, LNA amidites, and PMO monomers for ASO and siRNA drugs [13].

book_paragraphs: To understand how Sai Life Sciences actually makes money, you have to stop thinking of it as a single factory and start picturing a relay race with two batons. The first baton is the Contract Research Organization, or CRO—roughly 38% of revenue in the first half of FY27—where scientists help global drugmakers invent and test new molecules. The second baton is the Contract Development and Manufacturing Organization, or CDMO—the other 62%—where chemical engineers figure out how to cook those molecules safely, cleanly, and profitably in multi-ton reactors.

Notice where the customers sit: 100% of Sai Life's revenue comes from innovator molecules destined for regulated markets—roughly 40% from the United States, 35% from Europe, 15% from Japan, and 10% from the UK and other developed jurisdictions. There is zero exposure to low-margin domestic generics. Even more telling, revenue from top global pharmaceutical companies jumped from 28% in FY22 to 49% in FY26 as big pharma consolidated fragmented vendor lists into fewer, deeper strategic partnerships.

Let me make the CRO engine concrete for you. Think about Schrödinger, the New York computational drug discovery pioneer. Schrödinger's software can design thousands of promising virtual molecules on a screen, but software cannot test a molecule in a petri dish or check whether a mouse liver breaks it down too fast. In 2023, Sai Life built the dedicated Sai Schrödinger Research Laboratories right inside its Hyderabad campus. Dedicated FTE teams of Sai chemists and biologists run continuous Design-Make-Test-Analyze loops for Schrödinger, turning digital hypotheses into real physical compounds on recurring annual scientist-retainer contracts.

Why is that so valuable? Because in drug discovery, speed is everything. If an Indian vendor takes six weeks to ship a compound back to Boston for an assay, the research cycle stalls. By putting chemistry, biology, and DMPK under one roof in Hyderabad—and linking it to exploratory biology in Watertown near Boston—Sai Life compresses the feedback loop. That is why clients pay predictable FTE retainers rather than shopping every synthesis batch on price.

Now follow that baton into the CDMO engine. Suppose a Boston biotech or European pharma team discovers a promising oncology compound or an ADC cytotoxic payload. The lab recipe that made fifty grams for a mouse study might take twelve toxic steps and cost a fortune per gram. Sai Life's process chemists in Manchester, UK sit in the same time zone as European and East Coast CMC directors to reinvent that chemistry—replacing wasteful batch steps with continuous flow or enzymatic reactions.

Once the route is locked and Phase III clinical demand ramps up, technology transfers seamlessly to Bidar in Karnataka, where 920 kiloliters of reactors—ranging from nimble 250-liter trains up to 12,000-liter vessels, plus ultra-tight OEB 6 isolators for toxic oncology payloads—churn out commercial API for 34 approved or commercialized new chemical entities.

book_subsections.title: Why Modalities Matter More Than Tonnage
paragraphs: If you look at Sai Life's recent investments, they are not chasing bulk commodity tonnage. They are building a dedicated Peptide Research Center for GLP-1-era therapeutics using solid-phase, liquid-phase, and hybrid synthesis; manufacturing phosphoramidite and LNA monomers for RNA and oligonucleotide drugs; and synthesizing complex PROTAC protein degraders.

Each of these modalities requires specialized analytical characterization and multi-step purification where few Indian peers have full end-to-end scale. That complexity is what allows a mid-sized CRDMO to protect 28% operating margins without needing Divi's-style mega-tonnage.

book_subsections.title: The Pipeline Funnel Math
paragraphs: With roughly 160 active programs in development across Phase I through Phase III alongside 34 commercial NCEs, Sai Life's CDMO book has built-in diversification. Not every Phase II molecule survives clinical trials—attrition is a fact of biotech life—but having 34 commercialized molecules already generating recurring annual batches cushions the revenue base against single-trial failures.

book_subsections.title: How Discovery Chemistry Feeds Commercial Manufacturing Economics
paragraphs: It is easy to treat the 38% CRO segment and the 62% CDMO segment as two separate businesses, yet the real magic of Sai Life's model lies in the handoff between them. When a medicinal chemist in Hyderabad or a biologist in Watertown helps a client solve a solubility or toxicity bottleneck in Phase I, Sai Life's process team already understands the molecule's synthetic liabilities years before a Phase III RFP ever hits the market.

That early familiarity shortens tech-transfer timelines by months when a drug moves into clinical scale-up at Bidar. Even more importantly, it insulates Sai Life from pure price-per-kilogram bidding wars. Innovator pharma companies are loath to move a complex, multi-step synthesis—especially one involving OEB 6 containment or peptide coupling—to an unfamiliar vendor just to shave a few percentage points off batch cost when patent exclusivity clock is ticking.

book_subsections.title: Why Commercial Molecules Act Like Annuities Once Approved
paragraphs: Think about the economics of a commercialized New Chemical Entity from the perspective of a global pharma supply-chain head. Once a drug wins USFDA or EMA approval, the pharmaceutical company generates hundreds of millions—sometimes billions—of dollars in annual high-margin revenue. Saving ₹50 lakh on API synthesis by switching to an unproven contractor is irrational if it risks a single stock-out or regulatory query.

That asymmetry is why Sai Life's portfolio of 34 active commercial NCEs is so valuable. Each commercial molecule behaves like a multi-year manufacturing annuity that scales with global patient adoption, giving Bidar predictable base-load utilization that cushions the natural lumpiness of Phase I and Phase II clinical batches.

book_subsections.title: Inside the Bidar Reactor Trains: Flexibility as a Moat
paragraphs: Why does Sai Life highlight that its ~920 kiloliters of manufacturing capacity spans reactor sizes from 250 liters up to 12,000 liters across stainless steel, glass-lined, and Hastelloy vessels? Because innovator drug development rarely moves in a straight line from gram scale to ten-ton batches. A Phase II oncology therapy might require 400 liters of corrosive bromination chemistry in a Hastelloy train, while a Phase III cardiovascular molecule needs 8,000 liters of glass-lined hydrogenation.

By housing flexible, multi-material trains inside one USFDA- and PMDA-inspected campus at Bidar—and pairing them with OEB 6 high-containment isolators—Sai Life can keep a client's molecule in-house from first-in-human clinical supply all the way to commercial launch without forcing a risky plant transfer.

book_subsections.title: Why New Modalities Protect Long-Term Pricing Power
paragraphs: As small-molecule chemistry matures globally, Indian CRDMOs that only run standard commodity reactions face steady fee compression. Sai Life's early push into solid- and liquid-phase peptide synthesis, OEB 6 cytotoxic payloads for antibody-drug conjugates, and phosphoramidite monomers for RNA therapies positions the company in higher-complexity niches where analytical rigor—not cheap labor—determines who wins the contract.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: When you hear a CRDMO boast about 'integrated discovery-to-commercial capabilities,' always ask for the proof. In Sai Life's case, the proof is structural: Boston and Manchester win early intimacy with Western CMC and discovery heads, while Hyderabad and Bidar capture the 160-program pipeline at Indian engineering cost.
